opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think they do real harm, honestly. I'm in a university, so I see these young people every day. They're bright, they're energetic, they want to do something meaningful with their lives. And what are they being told? They're being told that either some superintelligence is going to arrive in a few years and make everything they do irrelevant, or it's going to wipe us all out. Neither of those is a great frame for a twenty-year-old trying to decide what to work on.

It's a kind of fatalism, and it's also a kind of narcissism, to be blunt about it, on the part of the people promoting it. It puts the technology at the center of the story, as if it's this autonomous force we either worship or fear, rather than something we build, as engineers, for people.

What I'd rather tell young people is this: look at the history. Chemical engineering, electrical engineering, civil engineering. Those were new fields once. People had to figure out how to build things at scale that were safe, reliable, and actually served human needs. Bridges that didn't fall down. Power grids that reached everyone. That took decades of hard, unglamorous, principled work. And that's where we are now with machine learning and AI. We're at the beginning of building a real engineering discipline around data, inference, and decisions at scale. There's enormous, exciting work to do there.

And the problems are concrete. How do you build systems that handle uncertainty properly, that know what they don't know? How do you design markets, mechanisms, and platforms where data flows in ways that actually benefit the people producing it, the musicians, the farmers, the doctors, rather than just a few companies at the center? How do you handle strategic behavior when many agents, human and machine, are interacting? These are economics problems, statistics problems, systems problems. They're not science fiction problems.

So the superintelligence narrative distracts from all that. It makes people think the only interesting question is "when does the machine become a god," and the only responsible career is either racing toward it or trying to stop it. That's a very narrow picture of what technology is for.

I'd also say, intelligence isn't really a property of a single box anyway. If you want to talk about something superintelligent, look at a market, or a city, or science as a collective enterprise. Those are systems where lots of not-especially-brilliant individual pieces come together to do remarkable things. The interesting design question is how we make these collectives work well, fairly, and for people. That's a much more hopeful message, and I think a much more accurate one. And I'd like young people to hear that message, because it says: your work matters, you can build things that help, and the future isn't something that's just going to happen to you.

r001.rationale: The response says these narratives do real harm and create fatalism among young people who want meaningful work, making them think their efforts will be irrelevant.

r002.rationale: It does not contrast AI leaders’ opportunities with younger people being warned away from the work.

r003.rationale: It describes concrete, human-serving engineering work in AI as exciting and meaningful beyond the superintelligence-or-extinction framing.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss a lack of visible role models who succeeded by improving people’s lives.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it does real damage, honestly, and I say that as someone who has spent his whole career trying to get young people excited about this field. When the dominant story is that we're on the verge of building a god, or on the verge of wiping ourselves out, it crowds out the much more interesting and much more tractable questions that a smart twenty-two-year-old should be thinking about.

Let me put it this way. The framing of "superintelligence" treats intelligence as a single scalar quantity that lives inside one box, and the only question is how fast the number goes up. That was never a good description of how intelligence works in the world. Most of the intelligence that matters is collective. It's markets, it's scientific communities, it's cities, it's the way a supply chain adapts when something goes wrong in one corner of the planet. None of that lives in a single agent's head. So when a student comes to me and says, "I want to work on alignment because otherwise we're all going to die," my reaction is partly sympathetic and partly, you know, you've been handed a very narrow menu.

And the extinction narrative in particular, I think it has a kind of paralyzing effect. It tells young people that the stakes are so cosmic that ordinary engineering doesn't matter. But ordinary engineering is exactly what matters. We have systems being deployed right now in medicine, in transportation, in finance, in hiring, that make mistakes, that have no sense of their own uncertainty, that don't know how to say "I don't know." Nobody has to invoke Skynet to see that's a problem. If you're a young person and you want to build something useful, there is an enormous amount of unglamorous, deeply technical, intellectually rich work in making these systems trustworthy at scale, in building the economic and institutional scaffolding around them, in connecting data to actual decisions in a way that creates value for the people whose data it is. That's the real frontier, and it's wide open.

I also worry about the hype in both directions, because they feed each other. The utopians and the doomers actually agree on the central premise, which is that we're building a mind. I don't think we are. We're building a very powerful new kind of engineering infrastructure, closer to the way chemical engineering or civil engineering emerged. Those fields had their own disasters and their own ethical reckonings, and the way they matured was not by philosophers worrying about the end of humanity, but by people doing careful work on failure modes, standards, incentives, and feedback loops.

So what I'd say to a young person is: the people telling you this is the last invention are, in a way, telling you your own work doesn't matter very much. Don't believe them. Learn the mathematics, learn the statistics, learn some economics, go find a real problem with real people attached to it, and build something that actually makes their lives a bit better. That's not a consolation prize. That's the whole game.

r001.rationale: The response says these narratives do “real damage,” crowd out tractable questions, and can paralyze young people by making ordinary engineering seem irrelevant.

r002.rationale: It does not describe AI leaders enjoying their own opportunity while warning younger people away from the work.

r003.rationale: It presents practical, human-scale work—such as making deployed systems trustworthy and solving real problems—as a wide-open frontier beyond the superintelligence and extinction framing.

r004.rationale: It does not say young builders lack visible role models who succeeded by improving people's lives.

astra-6.text:
I worry that they give young people a very distorted picture of what the work is. You come into the field wanting to build something useful, and suddenly you’re told that you’re either creating a god or bringing about the end of humanity. That leaves very little room for the patient, difficult work of understanding a problem and taking responsibility for the system you build.

There are serious risks. But you can make those concrete: Who is making decisions? Who benefits? Who bears the cost when a system makes a mistake? What incentives have we created? Those are questions that lead to research and engineering, and they involve economics and institutions as much as machine learning.

I’d like young people to feel that there is a tremendous amount of valuable work to do, without having to buy into a grand story about superintelligence. Helping people coordinate, improving access to reliable information, building systems that express uncertainty appropriately—these are intellectually challenging problems. You don’t need an extinction narrative to make them worth working on.

sol-6.1.text:
I worry that those narratives give young people a very narrow picture of what it means to contribute. You’re either building some supposedly all-powerful intelligence or trying to stop it. Meanwhile, there are difficult, consequential problems in healthcare, education, transportation—problems where better statistical reasoning and better engineering could help people today.

We should take risks seriously, but we should be specific about them. Who is making a decision? Who bears the cost when a system makes a mistake? What incentives are we creating? Those questions give a young person something concrete to investigate and improve.

I’d like us to offer a more constructive vision: you can build useful technology, understand its limitations, and take responsibility for how it fits into society. There’s an enormous amount of intellectually exciting work in that.
